name: Late-night eating cutoff

lead: The habit is to stop eating about three hours before bed.
Communities say it reduces puffiness and aids sleep. No studies were found testing that specific claim, though meal timing is an active research area.

paras: Proponents say a lighter digestive load at bedtime aids sleep; chrononutrition research links meal timing to circadian rhythms.
No documented harms; people with medical conditions affecting blood sugar are generally guided by clinicians on meal timing.

lead: The late-night eating cutoff is the practice of stopping food about three hours before bed. Proponents say it reduces morning facial puffiness and improves sleep.

Research on meal timing falls under chrononutrition, the study of how eating times interact with circadian rhythms. Wikipedia reports that epidemiological studies link late dinners with higher metabolic risk but that causality needs more research.[1]
No studies found testing a three-hour cutoff for puffiness or appearance.
infobox: Stop eating about 3 hours before bed

paras: Alain Delabos proposed in 1986 that larger meals belong earlier in the day and lighter ones in the evening. Later meals are associated with evening chronotype and postprandial hyperglycemia, and evening chronotypes with night eating.[1]
Rodent studies found that restricting food to the active phase reduced weight gain.[1]

No studies found on a three-hour pre-bed eating cutoff and facial puffiness. Observational chrononutrition research links late dinners and meal timing to metabolic outcomes, with causality still under study.[1]

lore.intro: The cutoff is discussed in looksmaxxing spaces as a way to wake up less puffy.

claims.claim: Stopping eating 3 hours before bed reduces puffiness and improves sleep
